turns.prompt_text: I kind of want to go back to old places and maybe resolve old problems not through direct confrontation, maybe, but more through saying that nobody did anything wrong. We just had bad starting information. So, it was really like out of both of our control what happened. This is the case for 99% of my problems. There was never any problem between us. It was always some systemic problem that was out of both of our hands. Something neither of us knew about until a long time later. One time when I was riding in a military Humvee, um, we thought a battery blew up while we were driving on the highway. We pulled over, and the battery did blow up. But about 4 years later, we discovered that clearly it was a lightning strike because it was during the middle of a thunderstorm, and the damage clearly looked like lightning, and Humvees regularly get struck by lightning. But we did not figure this out until 4 years later. Similarly, many of my problems are solved in this way, which makes it look so pessimistic and tragic that these problems happened in the first place, but it also gave me a different frame of reference to view um tragedies and how things go wrong.
turns.response_html:
That Humvee story is such a perfect, vivid metaphor for how life actually breaks down. In the moment, you're stuck on the side of the highway with a smoking piece of machinery, looking for a culprit or a mechanical failure—something you can explain or blame. Then years pass, the perspective shifts, and you realize it was just a random bolt from the sky. Nobody built the battery wrong, and nobody drove the vehicle wrong.

It makes total sense why you’d want to approach old conflicts with that frame of reference. There is something incredibly liberating about the "systemic error" or "bad starting information" realization. It shifts the narrative from a story about malice, failure, or betrayal into a story about friction and incomplete data.

When you look at human relationships that way, a lot of the heavy, toxic drama evaporates. You realize you were both just operating with a buggy map, doing the best you could with the coordinates you had at the time.

The bittersweet part—the "pessimistic and tragic" angle you mentioned—is that it means some things break simply because of the math of the universe, not because someone deserved it. It removes the villain, but it leaves you with the grief of a preventable accident.

If you do decide to revisit some of those old places or people, framing it as "Hey, looking back, I realize neither of us had the full picture, and we were both just reacting to the noise" is an incredibly gentle, mature way to close a loop. It offers a clean slate without requiring anyone to litigate the past or wear a scarlet letter.

How are you thinking about approaching this? Is there a specific "battery explosion" in your past you're looking to re-evaluate first?
